full_judgment:
petitioner, drawing our attention to the First Information Report annexed as annexure-A to the petition filed under section 561A of the CrPC firstly submits that, he appears in this case only for the accused No. 8. He then submits that the accused No. 8 is a General Manager of a private company limited by shares, namely Nordic Woods Ltd., which is engaged in the business of supply and that the a accused No. 8 petitioner is not a public servant. The learned Advocate further submits that, looking at the whole case, as narrated in the First Information Report (FIR) and assuming the same as true, no case, under any of the sections referred to in the FIR appears to have been made out so far the petitioner is concerned. In supported of his contention, the learned Advocate has taken us throughout the first information report and he has also cited the following decisions namely. State vs Md Nasim, Saifur Rahman and Abdur Razzaque reported in 2005 BLD (AD) 181 = 57 DLR (AD) 114, Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16, Akmol Hossain vs State reported in 40 DLR 483 and Nasiruddin Mahniud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14. He, therefore, strenuously argues that, so far as this petitioner is concerned, the impugned proceedings amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court and that for ends of justice further petitioner is concerned, the impugned proceedings amounts to an abuse of the process of the Court and that for ends of justice further prolongation of the impugned proceedings is not warranted in law. He, therefore, prayed for abashment of the impugned proceedings, so far as it relates to this petitioner. 

 6. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 2, referring to the contentions made in the petition under section 561A CrPC, mainly submits that, no cognizance has yet been taken by the trial Court in this case as the investigation could not be completed as yet, so the prosecution case is at a pre-matured stage and at this stage interference by this Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not called for and that the issues raised in the said petition are all disputed questions of facts which could be decided only by adducing evidence at the time of trial. The Court, hence there exists no scope for quashing the impugned proceedings. In sup-port of his contention, the learned advocate for the opposite party No. 2 has cited the following cases, namely, Nuruzzaman vs State report in 14 BLC 51; and Abdul Huque vs State reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1. 

 13. Now looking at the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner we find that, in 2005 BLD (AD) 181 = 57 DLR (AD) 114, between the State vs Mohammad Nasim it has been held that; "From the first information report or charge sheet it does not appear that the respondents obtained or attempted to obtain any pecuniary advantage abusing their position as Minster and Secretary of the Ministry of Home. In the whole deal we do not find any element of mens rea on the part of the respondents in as much as their actions appear to be bonafide. We are of the view that when the Tender Committee forwarded the matter to the Ministry with the opinion that the first lowest Tender stood disqualified for non-fulfillment of the condition of the Tender schedule, the Respondents (the Minister and Secretary) did not commit any offence agreeing to issue work order to the second lower Tenderer." We find close similarity between the facts and circumstances of the present case reported in 2005 BLD (AD) 181 = 57 DLR (AD) 114. Taking cognizance, we have looked into the decision cited on behalf of the ACC. In 60 DLR (AD) 1, it has been held by the Appellate Division that, "Before taking of cognizance of a case by the competent Court or tribunal a proceedings cannot be said to be pending and accordingly a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken and process issued." 

 19. Now, adverting to decisions of the Hon'ble Appellate Division, as cited by the contending parties, in deed, we have not found any conflict amongst the decisions cited before us, rather all these versatile decisions, read together, magnify and define the scope and propriety of interference under section 561A, CrPC. As such, it is the question of relevancy and of the propriety of the application of a particular decision that actually matters and that, undoubtedly, depends on the peculiarity of each particular case. As such, we do find authority for interference even before taking cognizance, if such interference is justifies in law, vide the case reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 114.
